title: Antennas: gain, length and patterns
blurb: How polarization, length, loading and gain decide where an antenna sends your signal.

T9A01.why: A beam antenna **concentrates** its signal in one direction, so it is strong that way and weak elsewhere.
T9A01.trap: "Beam" is about the signal, not the metal it is made of.

T9A02.why: Loading adds **inductance** (coils) so a physically short element behaves like a longer one.
T9A02.trap: A resistor wastes power as heat and does not lengthen anything.

T9A03.why: Polarization is the direction of the **electric field**, which follows the antenna's orientation.
T9A03.trap: The magnetic field is always present too, but it does not define polarization.

T9A04.why: A short, flexible antenna is a compromise on size, so it radiates **less efficiently** than a full-size quarter-wave.

T9A05.why: Shorter antenna, shorter wave it matches: the resonant frequency **rises**. Lengthening, coils and end loading all lower it.

T9A06.why: A **Yagi** is a beam, so it concentrates signal and has more gain than the all-around antennas listed.
T9A06.trap: An isotropic antenna is the zero-gain reference.

T9A07.why: The vehicle's metal body **shields** RF, so a handheld inside it sends and receives a weaker signal.

T9A08.why: On 2 m the wavelength is about 2 m, so a quarter-wave is a short whip of roughly **19 inches**.
T9A08.trap: A half-wave would be about twice as long.

T9A09.why: A 5/8-wave whip sends more signal toward the horizon, giving **more gain** than a quarter-wave.
T9A09.trap: The extra gain comes from a lower, not higher, takeoff angle.

T9A10.why: A dipole is a donut around the wire: strongest **broadside**, weakest off the ends.

T9A11.why: Gain is signal strength **in one direction compared with a reference antenna**. It does not add power.
T9A11.trap: The transmitter's output is unchanged: the signal is only redirected.
